2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Not applicable (retrospective documentary and institutional-historical case study of two municipal water systems across four defined historical periods with complete Table 2 matrix coverage; no human participant cohort subject to follow-up loss).
cross_tool_domains.confounding: High risk for causal attribution (though explicitly examined narratively): with N = 2 extreme cases and no counterfactual comparator, process tracing cannot statistically isolate polycentric governance features from major co-occurring structural factors (municipal wealth vs postindustrial fiscal distress, political power asymmetries, systemic racism, and individual executive leadership), although the authors explicitly trace these factors as interacting cross-cutting drivers (PDF pp. 4-6, 10-14).
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Adequate to strong: accurately distinguishes formal de jure legal structures from de facto enforcement norms across federal, state, and local instruments (U.S. Safe Drinking Water Act, 1989 Surface Water Treatment Rule, Filtration Avoidance Determinations, 1997 NYC Watershed Memorandum of Agreement, Michigan's revised Emergency Manager Law, and the federal Lead and Copper Rule), though legal rules are cited primarily via secondary literature, news journalism, and a USEPA Inspector General report rather than primary statutory/regulatory texts (PDF pp. 2, 7-12).
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Moderate concern: polycentricity is operationalized transparently via six structural and functional indicator questions (Table 1) coded independently by both authors to consensus across 24 case-period cells (Table 2), but categorical functional ratings (ADAPTIVE, MIXED, MALADAPTIVE) rely on unblinded retrospective qualitative judgment from secondary and journalistic sources without formal quantitative thresholds (PDF pp. 3-4, 9).
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Adequate: water system adaptation versus maladaptation is anchored in concrete regulatory, public health, and rate-affordability indicators drawn from official and secondary reports (e.g., EPA FAD renewals, 93% Whole Farm Planning participation, and $464/year average NYC bills vs Flint fecal coliform boil-water advisories, 87 Genesee County Legionnaires' disease cases, elevated water and child blood lead levels, and punitive water rates), though outcomes are synthesized narratively rather than measured uniformly across all four historical periods (PDF pp. 7-8).
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Moderate concern: no pre-registration or archival search protocol exists and historical narrative construction risks selective emphasis on confirmatory events (explicitly noted by the authors on PDF p. 14), although all six operationalized governance conditions are systematically reported across every case-period in Table 2 and the omission of Carlisle and Gruby's seventh enabling condition is transparently justified in Footnote 1 (PDF pp. 3, 9, 14).
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: High concern: purposive extreme-case selection on the dependent variable ('opposite ends of the SES performance continuum': NYC vs Flint) combined with non-systematic retrieval of secondary, journalistic, and publicly released FOIA documents introduces substantial case- and detail-selection bias, which the authors explicitly acknowledge (PDF pp. 1, 4, 14).

domain_ratings.justification: Core federal, state, and intergovernmental legal instruments—the Safe Drinking Water Act (and 1986 amendments), 1989 Surface Water Treatment Rule, Filtration Avoidance Determinations (FADs), 1997 NYC Watershed Memorandum of Agreement (MoA), Michigan's revised Emergency Manager Law, and the Lead and Copper Rule—are accurately characterized in functional terms and corroborated with official oversight findings (USEPA OIG Report No. 18-P-0221). However, primary statutory, regulatory (U.S.C./C.F.R./Michigan Public Act), and MoA clause citations are largely omitted in favor of secondary histories, academic articles, and news reports, with a minor name inconsistency ('Miguel del Toral' on p. 8 vs 'Miguel del Toro' on p. 11).

The paper precisely delineates the nested municipal, watershed/regional, state, and federal jurisdictions and agencies for both cases across two explicitly bounded historical eras each: New York City (BWS/NYCDEP), Croton and Catskills-Delaware watersheds, New York State executive/legislature, and USEPA (1900-1975 and 1976-present); and City of Flint, Genesee County, Detroit Water and Sewerage Department, Karegnondi Water Authority, State of Michigan (governor, treasurer, MDEQ), and USEPA Region 5 (1950-2012 and 2013-present).

Polycentric governance is clearly conceptualized and operationalized using six enabling conditions adapted from Carlisle and Gruby (2017), explicitly separating structural existence (PRESENT vs ABSENT) from functional operation (ADAPTIVE, MALADAPTIVE, or MIXED) via concrete indicator questions in Table 1, with Footnote 1 explaining why the seventh condition was omitted.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 2-4, 9 (Section 2, Footnote 1, Table 1, Section 3, Table 2)

domain_ratings.justification: System adaptation versus maladaptation ('desirable state' of drinking water SES performance) is substantiated with concrete regulatory compliance, contamination/health, and affordability indicators—such as multi-decade FAD renewals, 93% farm participation, and median household rates ($464/year) in NYC versus boil-water advisories, 87 Legionnaires' disease cases, 19x water corrosivity, residential and pediatric lead exposure, and double-national-average water bills in Flint—though synthesized qualitatively rather than via a single standardized metric across eras.

The authors transparently explain their purposive extreme-case rationale for choosing NYC and Flint (shared formal U.S. federalist governance structure paired with polar-opposite water system outcomes across critical historical junctures). However, they do not report search strings, inclusion criteria, or an itemized inventory for the documentary corpus (government inquiry reports, FOIA emails, white papers, news articles, and secondary histories).

Selecting two well-known extreme cases on the outcome variable ('two poles of the U.S. continuum of water system performance') and assembling case narratives from unsystematically sampled secondary and media accounts creates substantial case-selection and confirmation/detail-selection vulnerability, as explicitly noted in the Conclusion ('potential for selection bias in the choice of case details').
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 1, 4, 14 (Abstract, Section 3 Methods, Section 7 Conclusion)

domain_ratings.justification: Table 1 provides explicit structural and functional indicator questions for each of the six governance features, and Table 2 displays the complete 24-cell assessment matrix with concise cell-level rationales elaborated in Sections 5.1-5.6. Nevertheless, operational cutoffs distinguishing MIXED from predominantly ADAPTIVE or MALADAPTIVE ratings remain qualitative and interpretive.

Within-case historical process tracing and causal pathway diagrams (Figures 1-4) trace plausible temporal sequences, critical junctures (1997 NYC MoA; 2014 Flint water switch), and cross-scale feedback loops, but a two-case retrospective design lacking counterfactual controls cannot establish strong causal identification—a limitation the authors explicitly emphasize on pages 4 and 14.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 4-6, 14 (Section 3 Methods, Figures 1-4, Section 7 Conclusion)

domain_ratings.justification: While statistical adjustment is not applicable in small-N qualitative process tracing, the authors explicitly examine major historical and structural confounders—municipal wealth vs postindustrial decline, urban-rural and state-local power asymmetries, executive leadership agency, and institutional racism—integrating them into causal pathway diagrams (Figures 1-4) and cross-cutting thematic analysis rather than attributing outcomes solely to formal governance design.

Provides thorough, nuanced institutional analysis of multilevel American water federalism, tracing how formal rules interact with agency cultures, enforcement norms (EPA FAD vetting in NY vs Region 5 primacy deference in MI), state emergency financial receivership displacing local democratic accountability, litigation, and civil-society/academic mobilization.

The Table 1 operational questions and multi-period Table 2 coding layout offer a clear, reusable analytical template for comparative replication, and cited materials are publicly accessible, but the lack of a comprehensive primary-document/FOIA archive list and formal coding decision rules constrains exact independent replication.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 2-4, 9, 13-16 (Sections 1, 3, Table 1, Table 2, Section 7, References)

domain_ratings.justification: The Methods section reports that both researchers independently conducted process tracing and rated case expression of Table 1 indicators before resolving divergences via consensus discussion, which strengthens reliability over single-author narrative synthesis, though initial inter-coder agreement statistics and specific disagreed cells are not reported.

Although personal researcher positionality is not applicable/discussed for archival desk analysis, the authors display clear methodological reflexivity regarding interpretive discretion in pathway construction, explicitly warning that pathways could be traced differently using other case details and flagging selection bias and generalizability limits.

evidence_quotes.quote: The overarching set of rules for these systems stems from the U.S. Safe Drinking Water Act, which devolves authority and responsibility for national goals to state environmental agencies

evidence_quotes.criterion: Case sampling and selection strategy (D5, D6)
evidence_quotes.quote: Purposive sampling based on similarities and differences resulted in the selection of two municipal water systems: New York City and Flint, Michigan.

evidence_quotes.criterion: Independent coding and consensus procedure (D7, D12)
evidence_quotes.quote: Researchers independently engaged in a process tracing analysis and reached similar conclusions on case expression of Table 1 indicators. Where our findings diverged, we shared rationales and quickly arrived at consensus.
Case study data were collected from primary and secondary sources, including reports of government inquiries, utility reports, white papers, news articles

evidence_quotes.criterion: Causal identification and interpretive reflexivity (D8, D13)
evidence_quotes.quote: Conclusions are drawn tentatively, given the many ways that the pathways could be traced using different case details and the lack of counterfactuals for testing inferences.

evidence_quotes.criterion: Acknowledged selection bias and counterfactual limitations (D6, D8, D13)
evidence_quotes.quote: We offer conclusions with caveats regarding the potential for selection bias in the choice of case details, the lack of counterfactuals for testing causal inferences

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Biddle and Baehler (2019) conduct an ex post comparative institutional and legal-historical case study of two U.S. municipal drinking water systems—New York City (1900-1975 and 1976-present) and Flint, Michigan (1950-2012 and 2013-present)—using qualitative process tracing grounded in publicly available government inquiry reports, utility documents, FOIA emails, news coverage, law reviews, and secondary histories. Appraised under the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework (as a structured non-validated judgment, with no numeric composite score), the study exhibits strong conceptual operationalization of polycentricity (separating formal structural presence from adaptive/maladaptive function across six enabling conditions in Tables 1-2), strong jurisdictional and historical specificity, and rich institutional contextualization of U.S. Safe Drinking Water Act federalism, EPA Filtration Avoidance Determinations, the 1997 NYC Watershed Memorandum of Agreement, and Michigan's Emergency Manager receivership regime. Independent coding by two researchers with consensus reconciliation and candid methodological reflexivity further support credibility. However, internal validity for causal inference is inherently constrained by purposive selection on extreme poles of the outcome continuum (NYC vs Flint), non-systematic documentary source compilation with reliance on secondary/journalistic accounts rather than primary statutory citations, and the absence of counterfactual controls to isolate governance norms from major co-evolving confounders such as municipal wealth disparities, deindustrialization, power asymmetries, and leadership agency.
raw_response.overall_rating: Structured non-validated judgment: Moderate methodological quality (strong conceptual operationalization, jurisdictional specificity, and institutional context; adequate coding and measurement transparency; weak causal identification and high case-selection bias inherent to polar two-case historical process tracing)
raw_response.study_design_identified: Comparative institutional and legal-historical case study using ex post qualitative within-case process tracing across two purposively selected U.S. municipal water systems (New York City and Flint, Michigan) over two historical periods each
raw_response.where_found_summary: Design, purposive case selection, documentary data sources, independent dual-researcher coding of Table 1 indicators, and causal caveats are reported in Section 3 Methods (PDF p. 4) and Table 1 (PDF p. 3). Historical-institutional narratives and causal pathway diagrams appear in Section 4 and Figures 1-4 (PDF pp. 4-8). Comparative governance ratings appear in Section 5 and Table 2 (PDF pp. 8-12). Cross-cutting confounders and explicit study limitations (selection bias in case details, lack of counterfactuals, generalizability) are discussed in Sections 6-7 (PDF pp. 12-14).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: The study is an ex post comparative institutional and legal-historical case study spanning 1900-present (NYC) and 1950-present (Flint) based entirely on published histories, government inquiry reports, law reviews, news articles, and publicly released FOIA emails, with zero human subjects, interviews, or field recruitment. Because it lacks a quantitative quasi-experimental comparator arm (ruling out ROBINS-I) and involves retrospective institutional-legal process tracing rather than human-participant qualitative fieldwork (making CASP's participant recruitment, researcher-participant relationship, and human-research ethics items ill-fitting), the Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework is the exact design-matched instrument under RISK_OF_BIAS.md §§1-2.
